quote: Well, I don't know. I might have just popped up an ad sometime and replied to it, but, I have looked from time to time about solar for the house.
stewart_read: The customer gives a vague, low-conviction reason ('I don't know... might have popped up an ad'). Reactive read: rep should have probed further to surface a real motivator (bill pain, curiosity, etc.) before moving on. Strategic read: the rep may have judged there was no usable thread here and prioritized moving to verified data (address, roof) where he could build real momentum — which he then did successfully via the bill numbers. Given the rep never returns to interest at all, even loosely, during booking or button-up, the reactive read is better supported: this was a genuine miss, not a deliberate deferral, because there's no later moment where 'interest in solar' resurfaces as leverage.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep deliberately let the vague answer go because he planned to build genuine engagement later through the bill data, which he did — making the light touch here a correct sequencing choice rather than a miss.
coaching_implication: When a customer gives a shrug answer on interest, ask one follow-up (e.g., 'what got you looking into it — the bill, or just curiosity?') to bank a usable anchor for the appointment tieback and for the closer's handoff.

quote: Well, actually, the house is in a partnership with my sister and me, but I'm the general partner, the one who runs everything.
stewart_read: Customer discloses a co-owner (sister) on the title. Rep's response ('You're kind of, the boss there') accepts the customer's framing that he alone runs things and does not ask whether the sister should be included on the appointment.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have correctly judged that because the customer explicitly self-identified as the sole decision-maker ('the one who runs everything'), pursuing co-owner inclusion would have been unnecessary friction — unlike a spouse scenario where both parties typically must consent to a purchase.
coaching_implication: Even when a co-owner defers full authority to the customer, a quick check-in ('Does she need to be looped in for the actual decision, or are you good to move forward?') protects the appointment from a later 'let me check with my sister' stall at the closer stage.

quote: Well, good point. In the wintertime, it has gone to $500 a month. I just got one to this past month with a little over 200... somewhere between 3,500 and $4,000.
stewart_read: Customer hands over a rich, specific bill figure — a strong anchor for pain (annual cost, seasonal swing up to $500/month). Rep's response ('Oh, really? Okay. That makes sense... Thank you for kinda clarifying') acknowledges the number but files it rather than flipping it into an emotional or comparative frame ('so solar could level that $500 winter spike out'). Adjudicating strategic vs reactive: there is no later moment in the call where the rep references this figure again — not at booking, not at button-up — so this is a genuine missed flip rather than a deliberate deferral to the closer, since the rep had every opportunity in the button-up to tie the appointment to this pain point and did not.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep intentionally left the emotional flip for the closer, since setter scope is to gather data cleanly and let the specialist do the persuasion — but this doesn't hold because a light tieback at booking costs nothing and the schema explicitly frames capture-without-flip as the failure pattern.
coaching_implication: Practice one flip line after a strong bill number: 'so somewhere around $3,500-$4,000 a year just going to the utility — that's exactly what we'll build the design around.' Costs five seconds, banks the anchor for the customer's own motivation.

quote: On it says kilowatt hours and then it has the month. So you want the kilowatt hours per month?
stewart_read: Customer not only has his bill archived but proactively organizes and reads off a full 12-month usage history unprompted. This is a highly cooperative, detail-oriented customer profile — a strong signal of genuine intent, not just idle curiosity.
coaching_implication: Flag for the closer: this customer tracks and prints his own usage data monthly — he will likely want to engage with the technical detail of the proposal rather than a simplified summary. Worth noting in the handoff so the closer doesn't under-serve his level of engagement.

quote: Oh, yeah. So I'm actually in our Utah corporate office. So, it would just be two hours ahead. We are local to you. We're we have multiple offices in, the state of Virginia.
stewart_read: When the customer raises a time-zone/location question, the rep answers with specificity (Utah corporate office, but local Virginia offices named) rather than deflecting. This builds legitimacy through transparency in a moment that could otherwise seed suspicion.
coaching_implication: Good default behavior to reinforce: specific, honest answers to logistical questions build trust faster than vague reassurance. Worth naming as a positive example in the 1-on-1, not just a neutral pass.

quote: Okay. And we will do you a live request, just to double check that time still works for you. So just look out for that, so we're not calling you out of the blue.
stewart_read: Rep partially covers button-up: confirms a live-request follow-up and briefly touches on email access and not driving. But he never states the one-hour block, never gets the explicit 'is that fair?' handshake, and never gives a proper recap of the appointment specifics beyond day/time. This is a partial, not full, button-up.
coaching_implication: Add the missing pieces: state the hour-long block explicitly and close with a verbal handshake ('does that work for you?'). The current version books the slot but skips the mechanics shown to predict show-rate.
